newsitem.title: FRANCE: Channel Tunnel reopens for freight trains.
newsitem.headline: Channel Tunnel reopens for freight trains.

text.p: The Channel Tunnel reopened for freight trains on Thursday three days after a blaze on a train carrying trucks damaged the Franco-British undersea rail link, officials said.
"At 5:30 this morning (same GMT) the first freight trains ran into the tunnel from Britain to France," Eurotunnel SA Plc railway relations manager Jim Evans said.
Of the two trains, one was headed for Germany, the other for Spain. "We're back in business," Evans told BBC radio.

Eurotunnel officials in Calais said freight traffic was resuming in both directions after Monday's fire, that injured eight people after a truck caught fire aboard a train and forced an emergency halt in the 51 km (32 mile) tunnel.
Eurotunnel won permission early on Thursday from a 12-member Franco-British safety commission to run six trains in either direction in the tunnel every 90 minutes under a partial reopening.

The safety commission was holding new talks with Eurotunnel officials in Calais on Thursday to discuss resumption of other traffic -- trains shuttling trucks and cars and Eurostar passenger services between Paris and London and London and Brussels.
Eurotunnel officials said they hoped that the Eurostar service would be next to resume. "It's too early to say when," said Annabel Salmon, a spokeswoman for Eurotunnel.

Monday's fire caused extensive damage over about 800 metres (yards) of one of the twin rail tunnels. Full repairs are likely to take weeks. Eurotunnel hopes to get services up to two-thirds of normal despite the repairs.
The commission said it had decided to authorise freight trains after receiving assurances about security measures.
The Channel Tunnel is made up of separate tunnels handling northbound and southbound traffic with a third service tunnel in between. The three tunnels are linked by junction points.

Alain Bertrand, Eurotunnel's operations manager, told radio station France-Info-Frequence Nord on Wednesday night that he hoped Eurostar passenger trains and shuttle trains carrying private cars and their passengers in the 51-km (32-mile) tunnel might be rolling again before the end of the week.
Bertrand's statement contradicted a statement by the French SNCF railways which indicated passenger services would not resume until next week.

An SNCF statement said: "Taking account of the prolonged closure of the Channel Tunnel, the Eurostar (rail) service is completely suspended for an as yet undetermined period, which ought to include the weekend of November 23-24."
The fire on a lorry-carrying shuttle train unleashed a storm of criticism of the tunnel's much-vaunted safety systems.
Main roads in and around Calais were congested on Thursday with heavy lorries which would normally have used the tunnel but were instead trying to embark on ferries.

Eurotunnel said damage in the tunnel was worse than first feared, with buckled tracks, cracked concrete and damage to electrical cables. Full repairs are likely to last weeks and cost millions of pounds (dollars).

The only trains which ran in the tunnel on Wednesday were shuttling staff. The closure to paying clients means a loss of revenues of about a million pounds ($1.7 million) a day, a pinprick compared to the company's nine billion pounds ($15 billion) in debts.
